title: Students Don't Want to Write Like Robots
author: Curious Pedagogy
summary: George, a writing professor with 25 years of experience, designed a course on Writing with AI in which the first assignment asked students to produce academic essays that didn't seem AI-generated—forcing them to understand, from the inside, how AI produces text. The resulting guide (co-created with students) identifies seven tells of AI writing: falsified sources, weak use of detail, flawless grammar (without the structural breakdowns humans produce at the limits of understanding), lack of verbal awkwardness, inappropriate tour-guide tone, odd structure and formatting choices, and sophisticated language paired with shallow conclusions. The most important insight: AI generates text through pattern prediction, with no ideas, while humans start with ideas and learn grammar to express them. When students were forced to write like LLMs, they found it awful—they had no way to evaluate whether they'd said something intelligent or gibberish, and felt no attachment to the result. They unanimously said they'd rather write like humans.
points: Seven tells of AI-generated academic writing: falsified sources, weak use of detail, flawless grammar, lack of verbal awkwardness, inappropriate confident tone, odd formatting choices, and sophisticated writing paired with shallow conclusions.
Structural grammar errors—sentences that spiral into incoherence—are actually signs of human learning: they happen when a writer is thinking at the very limits of their understanding.

AI generates text based on what its algorithm predicts the thing you're asking for should sound like; it's good at producing words that sound like academic writing but can't produce words that reflect sophisticated thought.

When students let AI alter their word choice and sentence structure too heavily, they end up with a writing style out of sync with their own ideas—which leads to bad writing regardless of whether it's flagged as AI.

When forced to produce AI-generated essays, students found the process torturous and the product meaningless—they couldn't tell if they'd written something intelligent or gibberish, and felt no ownership of the work.
quotes: Since AI can’t really read things or come to conclusions of its own, it’s bad at working with fine details.

When we think at the very limits of our understanding (otherwise known as the Zone of Proximal Development or the place where learning happens), we struggle to articulate what we’re thinking, and so our grammar breaks at the points where our understanding falters.
AI is very good at sounding sophisticated, but in practice AI writing is usually quite shallow.

Humans start with ideas, and then we learn the grammar and vocabulary we need to express those ideas. For humans, writing with correct and sophisticated grammar is actually a high-end skill we might spend a lifetime mastering.

AI generates text based on what its algorithm predicts the thing you're asking for should sound like, and it's pretty good at producing words that sound like academic writing. But since it can't think, it's pretty bad at producing words that appear to reflect sophisticated human thoughts.

In effect, George had forced them to write like LLMs, and they found it awful. He felt a little guilty for that, but it’s also hard not to feel a little chuffed when a room full of students, given a real taste of what it means to write like an AI, unanimously decide that they’d rather write like humans.
